b.t: Read each section slowly, out loud. German spelling is much more regular than English spelling: once you know the rules in section 1.4, you can pronounce almost every word correctly the first time you see it. That is why this book starts with sounds before grammar.

Every German sentence has a speaker button, and a small slow button next to it that plays it at a slower pace. At the top of the page you can choose a male or a female voice and switch the English translations on or off. A good habit: cover the translation, read the German, then check.
At the end of each section you will find exercises. They tell you why an answer is right or wrong, so do not skip the explanations. They are part of the lesson.
Anna and Raj meet on the first day of a German course in Berlin. Read the dialogue once for meaning, then again aloud.
Anna and Raj meet at the entrance of the language school.
Anna: Hallo! Ich heiße Anna. Und du?
b.g: Hi! My name is Anna. And you?

b.t: Raj: Hallo, Anna. Ich heiße Raj.
b.g: Hi, Anna. My name is Raj.

b.t: Anna: Woher kommst du, Raj?
b.g: Where do you come from, Raj?

b.t: Raj: Ich komme aus Indien. Und du?
b.g: I come from India. And you?

b.t: Anna: Ich komme aus Deutschland. Wie geht's?
b.g: I come from Germany. How are you?

b.t: Raj: Gut, danke. Und dir?
Anna: Auch gut. Tschüss, Raj!
Raj: Tschüss, Anna! Bis morgen!

Three things to notice before we go on. First, there is no word for "am" in "my name is": German says Ich heiße Anna, literally "I am-called Anna". Second, du is used between two students: it is the informal "you". Third, Wie geht's? is short for Wie geht es dir?, literally "How goes it to you?". You will see why it is dir and not du when we meet the dative case later in the book.

Achtung: In writing, the greeting is capitalised: Guten Morgen. Greeting words are not a place where English helps you: there is no German word for "good afternoon". Use Guten Tag until the evening.

Bitte, danke, Entschuldigung
Three little words do a lot of work in everyday life.
• danke means "thank you". The polite reply is bitte.
• bitte has two jobs: it means "please" when you ask for something, and "you're welcome" when you answer danke. English needs two words; German uses one.
• Entschuldigung means "excuse me" (to get attention) and "sorry" (for a small mistake). For something more serious, say Es tut mir leid, "I'm sorry".
Einen Kaffee, bitte.
Danke! – Bitte!
Entschuldigung, wie bitte?
Ja, bitte.
Nein, danke.
Tipp: When you do not understand something, say Wie bitte? ("Pardon?"). It is polite and every German speaker understands it immediately.

The alphabet
German uses the same 26 letters as English, plus ä, ö, ü (called Umlaute) and ß (called Eszett or "scharfes S").

b.t: To spell a word aloud, say the letter names in a row. On the phone you will also hear spelling words ("A wie Anton"), but the plain letter names are enough for now.
Vowels: long or short
Every vowel has a long and a short version. The rule of thumb that works most of the time:
• A vowel is long before one consonant, before h, or when it is doubled: Name /ˈnaːmə/, Sohn /zoːn/, Tee /teː/.
• A vowel is short before two or more consonants: Land /lant/, kommen /ˈkɔmən/, Mutter /ˈmʊtɐ/.
The h after a vowel is silent. It only tells you the vowel is long: Zahl /tsaːl/, Uhr /uːɐ̯/.

b.t: An unstressed e at the end of a word is a soft "uh", as in the "a" of "about": Name /ˈnaːmə/, bitte /ˈbɪtə/.
The umlauts ä, ö, ü
These three sounds do not exist in English, so they are worth practising.
• ä is almost the same as short e: Männer, Käse. When it is long it sounds like the "e" in "pet" held longer: Käse /ˈkɛːzə/.
• ö: say "eh" and round your lips as if saying "oh". It sounds a bit like the vowel in "bird" with no r: schön /ʃøːn/, Köln.
• ü: say "ee" and round your lips as if saying "oo". für /fyːɐ̯/, Tschüss /tʃʏs/, grün.
If your keyboard cannot type them, write ae, oe, ue instead (schoen, Tschuess) and ss for ß. Native speakers do exactly this in emails and passwords.
The letter ß
ß is simply a double s. It appears after long vowels and diphthongs: heißen /ˈhaɪ̯sn̩/, Fuß, groß. After a short vowel you write ss: Wasser, muss. There is no capital ß in everyday writing.

b.t: The two sounds of ch are really one letter pair with two neighbours: the ich-sound after "front" vowels and the ach-sound after "back" vowels. A good test is the pair ich / ach: say them one after another and feel where your tongue is.
Merke: Final devoicing. At the end of a word, b, d, g are pronounced as p, t, k: Tag /taːk/, und /ʊnt/, Land /lant/, ab /ap/. In the plural the sound returns: Tage /ˈtaːɡə/.
Where is the stress?

Almost every German word is stressed on the first syllable: Ma-ma, Na-me, Ta-ge. There are two common exceptions you will meet early: words that begin with be-, ge-, ver-, er- put the stress on the next syllable (be-zah-len, Ge-mü-se), and many words borrowed from French or Latin are stressed late (Stu-dent, Tele-fon).

Merke: - German is spelled regularly. ei = "eye", ie = "ee", eu = "oy", au = "ow", w = v, v = f, z = ts, j = y, sch = sh, sp/st = shp/sht at the start of a word. - A vowel before one consonant is long, before two it is short. Kultur: Landeskunde: where is German spoken? German is the official language of Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein, and one of four official languages in Switzerland (alongside French, Italian and Romansh). It is also spoken in parts of Italy (South Tyrol), Belgium and Luxembourg. Each region has its own greetings and accent, but the written standard you are learning is the same everywhere.
Learn the nouns with their article and plural. The vocabulary also appears in your Glossar, where you can review it with flashcards.

b.t: The same question, Wie heißen Sie? or Wie heißt du?, can sound very different depending on who you are talking to. Read both dialogues aloud, then notice how every verb changes.
Frau Weber is a teacher. Raj Patel arrives for his first lesson. They have never met.
Frau Weber: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie?
b.g: Good day! What is your name?

b.t: Herr Patel: Guten Tag. Ich heiße Raj Patel.
b.g: Good day. My name is Raj Patel.

b.t: Frau Weber: Woher kommen Sie, Herr Patel?
b.g: Where do you come from, Mr Patel?

b.t: Herr Patel: Ich komme aus Indien. Und Sie?
b.g: I come from India. And you?

b.t: Frau Weber: Ich komme aus Österreich, aber ich wohne in Berlin.
b.g: I come from Austria, but I live in Berlin.

b.t: Herr Patel: Sprechen Sie Hindi?
Frau Weber: Nein, aber ich spreche Englisch und Deutsch.
b.g: No, but I speak English and German.

b.t: Anna and Raj sit next to each other in class.
Anna: Wie heißt du?
Raj: Ich heiße Raj. Und du?
b.g: My name is Raj. And you?

b.t: Anna: Ich heiße Anna. Wo wohnst du?
b.g: My name is Anna. Where do you live?

b.t: Raj: Ich wohne in Berlin. Und du?
b.g: I live in Berlin. And you?

b.t: Anna: Ich auch. Wie alt bist du?
b.g: Me too. How old are you?

b.t: Raj: Ich bin vierundzwanzig. Und du?
Anna: Ich bin zweiundzwanzig.

What changed between the two conversations? Sie with -en verbs (heißen Sie, kommen Sie, sprechen Sie) versus du with -st verbs (heißt du, wohnst du). The rest of the chapter explains why, one piece at a time.

pages.t: K2 · 2.2 Personal pronouns: who is doing it?

b.t: A pronoun replaces a noun. If you say Anna wohnt in Berlin. Sie ist Studentin., the word sie replaces Anna. German chooses the pronoun by person (first, second, third), number (one or more) and, for the third person, gender.

ja: 私, I
倒れる, 水

b.t: Four points are worth a closer look.

1. ich is not capitalised unless it begins a sentence. Du and ihr are written with small letters in normal text. 2. German has two kinds of "you" for one person (du and Sie) and one extra for several people (ihr). English you covers all of them. 3. Sie (formal "you") is always written with a capital S, in every position in the sentence. That is the main way to tell it apart from sie (she, they) on the page. 4. sie has three meanings: she, they and (capitalised) Sie = formal you. In speech they sound identical. The verb ending tells you which one it is:
Sie kommt aus Indien.
Sie kommen aus Indien.
b.g: They come from India. / You (formal) come from India.

b.t: Kommen Sie aus Indien?

b.t: Merke: Grammatical gender and natural gender are different things. er, sie, es replace nouns by their grammatical gender, not only by the sex of a person. A table is der Tisch, so you say er for it. You will learn how to find a noun's gender in chapter 3. For now, use er for a man, sie for a woman and es for a child or a thing like das Auto ("it").
This is the first real cultural decision a learner has to make, and it is easier than it sounds.
• Use du with friends, family, children, pets, fellow students and, in many workplaces and clubs, colleagues. Online, du is the standard.
• Use Sie with strangers, officials, shop staff, your teacher, your boss and anyone older than you whom you do not know well.
• If in doubt, use Sie. Nobody will mind that you are too polite. Being too casual to a stranger can sound rude.
• The switch to du is usually offered by the older or more senior person: Wollen wir uns duzen? ("Shall we use du?"). It is also fine to ask.
• Sie goes with Herr/Frau + surname: Frau Weber, Herr Patel. Du goes with first names.

Kultur: Moving from Sie to du is a small social event in German-speaking countries. People sometimes celebrate it with a drink: das Du anbieten, "to offer the du". Don't be surprised if a colleague uses du from day one: many start-ups, universities and Scandinavian-style companies do. When you meet someone in a shop, at the post office or on the phone for the first time, Sie is the safe choice.

Englisch ↔ Deutsch: English how and German wie look alike but are not always the same: you ask for someone's name with wie (Wie heißt du?), literally "How are you called?". Don't say Was ist dein Name? when you can say Wie heißt du?; both are correct, but the second is much more natural.
Yes/no questions
If the answer is ja or nein, the verb comes first. There is no extra word like English "do".
Kommst du aus Indien?
Wohnen Sie in Berlin?
Sind Sie Herr Patel?
Ist Anna müde?
You can answer in full or briefly: Ja, ich komme aus Indien. or just Ja. If the answer is no: Nein, ich komme aus Deutschland.

In a normal German statement the conjugated verb is always in second position. That means second position in the sentence, not necessarily the second word. The first position can hold the subject or something else. When something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves behind the verb.

b.t: Both Ich wohne in Berlin and In Berlin wohne ich mean the same thing. The second is slightly more emphatic: "It's in Berlin that I live."
Merke: Verb second. In statements and in W-questions the conjugated verb stands in position 2. In yes/no questions it stands in position 1.
Saying "not": nicht
Nicht negates the verb or the whole statement and normally goes at the end:
Ich komme nicht aus Indien.
Ich arbeite heute nicht.
Anna ist nicht müde.
When you simply contradict a statement, you can also answer with nein: Kommst du aus China? – Nein, ich komme nicht aus China. The word kein ("no / not a") is introduced in chapter 3.

German has two negations, and choosing the right one is easy once you know the rule.
• kein negates a noun that has ein/eine or no article: Ich habe ein Auto → Ich habe kein Auto.
• nicht negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, places, nouns with der/die/das or mein/dein.

r: Das ist ein Hund. → Das ist kein Hund. · Ich habe Zeit. → Ich habe keine Zeit.
Ich arbeite nicht. · Anna ist nicht müde.
Das ist nicht der Hund. · Das ist nicht mein Bruder.

Another small word that helps: answering a negative question. If someone asks Hast du keine Schwester? ("Don't you have a sister?"), the German doch means "yes, I do": Doch, ich habe eine Schwester. And nein means "no, I don't". English has no one-word equivalent.

The prefix always sits at the end of a statement, however long the sentence becomes. In yes/no questions the verb comes first and the prefix is still last: Stehst du früh auf?
How do I know if a prefix separates?

Prefixes that are words on their own, mostly prepositions and adverbs, separate: an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, ab-, fern-, zurück-. A second group of prefixes never separates: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-. Those verbs behave like any other verb: Ich verstehe dich. Ich bekomme einen Brief.
A useful clue is stress: in a separable verb the stress is on the prefix (AUFstehen), in an inseparable verb it is on the stem (beKOMmen).

Merke: - Days, months, seasons are masculine and capitalised. am + day or part of the day, im + month or season, um + clock time. - Time: official = Uhr + minutes (dreizehn Uhr fünfzehn). Everyday = nach / vor / Viertel / halb. halb acht = 7:30. - Separable verbs split: conjugated verb in position 2, prefix at the end. Kultur: Landeskunde: punctuality and rest. Being on time (pünktlich) matters in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, for appointments and trains alike. b.t: Three ways to say what you like.
1. mögen, "to like", is another modal verb, used with a noun: Ich mag Käse. Er mag keinen Fisch. (Forms: ich mag, du magst, er mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie mögen.)
2. gern is placed after the verb and means "with pleasure", so any verb can "like": Ich esse gern Pizza. Ich trinke gern Tee. Its negative is nicht gern.

b.t: Es gibt + accusative means "there is / there are". It is always singular (gibt), whatever follows. You use it to ask what a place has, and to say what is available:

Hundreds work like the tens: hundert, zweihundert, dreihundert … and tausend (1000). The smaller number follows without und: hundertzwanzig (120), zweihundertfünfundfünfzig (255). Everything is one word.

Kultur: Landeskunde: shopping. Shops are usually closed on Sundays, and in many towns also in the evening. Supermarkets open until 20:00 or 22:00 on weekdays. For bottles you pay a deposit (Pfand), which you get back at the machine in the supermarket. Seasonal sales are called Schlussverkauf (the summer and winter sales). If you do not like what you bought, ask about Umtausch (exchange) before you pay.

Kultur: Landeskunde: getting around. Public transport in German-speaking cities is dense and punctual, and a monthly pass (such as the Deutschlandticket) covers local trains and buses across the country. On many buses and trams you must buy and validate your ticket before you board (entwerten, to stamp it). Riding without a valid ticket (Schwarzfahren) can cost around 60 €. Pedestrians wait at a red light even on an empty street, and cyclists use their own lanes. When you ask a stranger for the way, use Sie and start with Entschuldigung: it is polite and everyone understands it.

b.t: Look at the patterns:
• ich and er/sie/es are always identical, and carry no ending: ich kann, er kann.
• The singular has a different vowel from the plural: können → kann, müssen → muss, dürfen → darf, wollen → will. The plural, and the infinitive, are regular.
• sollen has no vowel change.
The second verb goes to the end
The modal is the conjugated verb, so it stays in position 2. The main verb goes to the very end, in the infinitive:
Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
Wir wollen am Wochenende ins Kino gehen.
Darf ich hier sitzen?
This is the same bracket you saw with separable verbs. With a separable verb, the infinitive is written as one word: Ich muss früh aufstehen. (not "auf stehen").

Merke: Modal + infinitive at the end. The modal verb is conjugated and in position 2 (or position 1 in a yes/no question). The other verb stays in the infinitive and goes to the end: Ich möchte Deutsch lernen. Kannst du mich anrufen? Wir müssen jetzt gehen.
You can leave the infinitive out when it is obvious: Ich kann Deutsch. (= Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.), Ich muss nach Hause. (= ... gehen).

Kultur: Landeskunde: travelling. Germany, Austria and Switzerland are together called D-A-CH, after their international car codes D, A and CH. Famous holiday regions are the Alps for hiking and skiing, the North Sea and Baltic Sea (Nordsee, Ostsee) for beaches, and the Black Forest (Schwarzwald). In hotels, breakfast is often a buffet and included. In Germany a Jugendherberge (youth hostel) welcomes people of all ages. For rail travel, you can often save money with a Sparpreis ticket if you book in advance. pages.t: K11 · 11.2 How the perfect tense works

b.t: German has several past tenses. In everyday speech and messages you use the Perfekt, built from two parts:
haben / sein (conjugated, position 2) + participle (Partizip II, at the end)
Ich habe gestern Fußball gespielt.
Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren.
The helper verb is conjugated. The participle never changes. And the participle goes to the end of the sentence, the same bracket as with modal verbs and separable verbs.
The perfect covers all English past forms: Ich habe gearbeitet means "I worked", "I have worked" and "I was working".

Merke: - Perfekt = haben / sein (position 2) + participle (end). It translates every English past form. - Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, gelernt, gearbeitet). - Strong verbs: ge- + stem + -en, often with a vowel change (gegessen, getrunken, geschrieben, gegangen). Learn them with the participle. - Separable: ge in the middle (aufgestanden, eingekauft, angerufen). - No ge-: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, zer- and -ieren (besucht, verstanden, telefoniert). - sein for movement and change of state (gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, aufgestanden) and for sein itself; haben for the rest. - war / hatte for sein / haben, schon / noch nicht for already / not yet.

Kultur: Landeskunde: spoken and written German. In Germany you hear Ich habe gegessen but you read er aß in a novel. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people use the Perfekt even more, and often avoid the Präteritum altogether, except for war and hatte. The word gestern is useful in any context, and so are vorgestern (the day before yesterday) and heute Morgen (this morning).

Kultur: Landeskunde: work and health. In Germany nearly everyone has health insurance (Krankenversicherung) and shows an insurance card at the doctor's. You usually need an appointment (Termin); in emergencies, 112 is the number for the fire brigade and ambulance, and 110 is for the police. If you are ill and cannot work, your employer expects a doctor's note (Krankmeldung). Pharmacies (Apotheken) are marked with a red letter A, and one is always open at night in each area (Notdienst). At work, colleagues use Sie and surnames at first; many workplaces move to du and first names once people know each other.

The next level, A2, builds on exactly the foundation you have now. In A2 you will work on:
• Subordinate clauses with weil, dass, wenn, obwohl (verb at the end of the clause).
• Adjective endings (ein großer Tisch, die kleine Katze).
• Comparison (größer, am größten, besser, am besten).
• Reflexive verbs (sich freuen, sich treffen) and more separable verbs.
• The genitive (das Auto meines Bruders), relative clauses (der Mann, der …) and the future with werden.
• Connected writing: emails, descriptions, opinions.

Merke: You have completed A1. If you can do the tasks in 13.4 without much help, you are ready for the Goethe-Zertifikat A1 and for A2. Even five minutes a day of reading aloud will change how you sound.

Kultur: Landeskunde: the Goethe-Zertifikat A1. The Goethe-Institut's A1 exam, Start Deutsch 1, is accepted by embassies for family reunification in Germany. It has four parts of 25 points each, 100 points in total, and you pass with 60 (and all four parts taken). The exam takes about 80 minutes. Examination centres exist all over the world, and there are alternative certificates from telc and ÖSD. Whatever exam you choose, the best preparation is the same: listen, read, write and speak a little every day.
